source_text: Τότε δὴ πολλῶν ὑποβρυχίων γινομένων, καὶ τοῦ χειμῶνος αἰρομένου, καὶ πολλῶν ναυαγούντων, ὁ μακάριος οὗτος Ῥωμανὸς παρελθὼν εἰς μέσους οὐκ ἐσκόπησεν εὐθέως, ὅπως ἑαυτὸν ἐπιδῷ τοῖς κινδύνοις, ἀλλὰ πρότερον τοὺς πεφοβημένους, τοὺς ἀναπεπτωκότας, τοὺς τὴν οἰκείαν προδόντας σωτηρίαν συνῆγε, παρεθάῤῥυνεν, ἀναμαχέσασθαι παρεσκεύαζε, τοὺς μὲν καταπεσόντας ἀνορθῶν, τοὺς δὲ ἑστῶτας ἀσφαλιζόμενος εὐχαῖς, καὶ παραινέσεσι, καὶ συμβουλαῖς, περὶ τῶν μελλόντων, περὶ τῶν παρόντων πραγμάτων πολλὰ φιλοσοφῶν, δεικνὺς τὸ πρόσκαιρον τούτων, τὸ διηνεκὲς ἐκείνων, ἀντιτιθεὶς τοῖς πόνοις τὰ ἔπαθλα, ταῖς βασάνοις τοὺς στεφάνους, ταῖς ἀλγηδόσι τὰ βραβεῖα, διδάσκων τίς μὲν ἡ παροῦσα ζωὴ, τίς δὲ ἡ μέλλουσα, καὶ πόσον ἑκατέρας τὸ μέσον, καὶ ὅτι πάντως ἀποθανεῖν ἀνάγκη· κἂν γὰρ μὴ τούτῳ τῷ τρόπῳ καταλύσωμεν τὴν ζωὴν, τῷ νόμῳ τῆς φύσεως πάντως ἀναγκαζόμενοι μικρὸν γοῦν ὕστερον τῶν σωμάτων ἀποστησόμεθα τούτων. Ταῦτα δὴ καὶ τὰ τούτοις ἐοικότα παραινῶν ἀνώρθωσε τὰς παρειμένας χεῖρας, ἐστήριξε τὰ παραλελυμένα γόνατα, τοὺς φυγάδας ἐπανήγαγε, τὴν δειλίαν ἐξέβαλε, τὴν ἀγωνίαν ἀπήλασε, θάρσος ἐνέθηκεν, ἀντὶ δειλῶν προθύμους ἐποίησεν, ἀντὶ δορκάδων καὶ ἐλάφων λέοντας ἀπειργάσατο πολλῆς πνέοντας τῆς ἰσχύος, συνεκρότησε τοῦ Χριστοῦ τὸ στρατόπεδον, τὴν αἰσχύνην τὴν παρ' ἡμῖν εἰς τὰς τῶν πολεμίων μετήνεγκε κεφαλάς. Ἰδὼν τοίνυν ὁ διάβολος ἀθρόαν μεταβολὴν γεγενημένην, καὶ τοὺς χθὲς καὶ πρῴην δεδοικότας αὐτὸν καὶ τρέμοντας, νῦν καταγελῶντας αὐτοῦ καὶ κατατολμῶντας, ἐπαποδυομένους τοῖς κινδύνοις, ἐπιπηδῶντας τοῖς κολαστηρίοις, καὶ γνοὺς τὸν αἴτιον, πάντας ἀφεὶς, κατ' ἐκείνου λοιπὸν ἔπνευσεν ὅλος, πᾶσαν τὴν δύναμιν αὐτοῦ καὶ τὴν μανίαν κατὰ τῆς μακαρίας ταύτης κινῶν κεφαλῆς. Καὶ τί ποιεῖ; Σκοπεῖτε τὴν κακουργίαν. Οὐκ ἤγαγεν αὐτὸν ἐπὶ βασάνους, οὐκ ἀπέτεμεν αὐτοῦ τὴν κεφαλήν· ἐδίδαξε γὰρ αὐτὸν ὁ παρελθὼν χρόνος, ὅτι πάντα ταῦτα εἰκῆ καὶ μάτην ἐγίνετο. Οὐ γὰρ μόνον οὐκ ἐνέκοψε τῶν πεπιστευκότων τὴν προθυμίαν, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐπέτεινε πλέον, καὶ μείζω καὶ θερμοτέραν αὐτὴν ἐποίησεν. Ἄνθρακας ὑπεστόρεσα, φησὶν, οἱ δὲ ὡς ἐπὶ ῥόδα ἔτρεχον· πῦρ ἀνῆψα, οἱ δὲ ὡς εἰς πηγὰς ὑδάτων ψυχρῶν ἑαυτοὺς ἔῤῥιψαν· κατέξανα τὰς πλευρὰς, καὶ βαθείας ἀνέτεμον αὔλακας, καὶ κατήγαγον ῥύακας αἱμάτων, οἱ δὲ ὡς χρυσίῳ πάντοθεν περιῤῥεόμενοι, οὕτως ἐκαλλωπίζοντο· τοῖς κρημνοῖς ἔῤῥιψα, καὶ εἰς πέλαγος κατεπόντισα, οἱ δὲ οὐχ ὡς εἰς βυθὸν καταβαίνοντες, ἀλλ' ὡς εἰς αὐτὸν ἀναβαίνοντες τὸν οὐρανὸν, οὕτω διέκειντο σκιρτῶντες, καὶ ἀγαλλόμενοι, καὶ ὥσπερ ἐν ἱερᾷ πομπῇ χορεύοντες, καὶ ἐν λειμῶνι παίζοντες χλοερῷ, οὕτω τὰς τιμωρίας ἕκαστος ἥρπαζον, οὐχ ὡς τιμωρίας, ἀλλ' ὡς ἄνθη λαμβάνοντες ἐαρινὰ, καὶ στεφανούμενοι, καὶ τῇ τῆς οἰκείας προθυμίας ὑπερβολῇ τὰς ἐμὰς προέφθανον τιμωρίας. Τί τοίνυν ἂν εἴη πρακτέον, φησίν; Ἀποτέμω τούτου τὴν κεφαλήν; Ἀλλ' ὅπερ εὔχεται, τοῦτο γίνεται, καὶ μείζονα λαμβάνουσιν οἱ μαθηταὶ τὴν διὰ τῶν ἔργων παραίνεσιν· καὶ γὰρ παρῄνεσεν, ὅτι μαρτύρων θάνατος οὐκ ἔστι θάνατος, ἀλλὰ ζωὴ πέρας οὐκ ἔχουσα, καὶ μάλιστά γε ὑπὲρ ταύτης πάντα ὑπομένειν χρὴ, καὶ ὅτι δεῖ καταφρονεῖν τελευτῆς. Ἂν τοίνυν ἀποτέμω τὴν κεφαλὴν, καὶ γενναίως ἐνέγκῃ τὸ συμβὰν, διὰ τῶν ἔργων αὐτοὺς παιδεύσει σαφέστερον, ὅτι οὕτω θανάτου δεῖ καταφρονεῖν, καὶ μᾶλλον αὐτῶν ἀνορθώσει τὰ φρονήματα, καὶ πλείονα αὐτοῖς ἐμπνεύσει τελευτήσας τὴν προθυμίαν.
thought_title: Romanus strengthens the wavering; the devil's scheme
orientation: Chrysostom is describing how Romanus, during the persecution, first encouraged and strengthened his fellow Christians before offering himself to danger, and then how the devil, seeing this, turned all his fury against Romanus alone.
pass_a_gloss: Then indeed, when many were being submerged, and the storm was rising, and many were suffering shipwreck, this blessed Romanus, coming forward into the midst, did not consider at once how he might give himself over to the dangers, but first he gathered together those who were afraid, those who had fallen back, those who had betrayed their own salvation, he encouraged them, he prepared them to fight back, raising up those who had fallen, and securing those who were standing with prayers and exhortations and counsels, philosophizing much about the things to come and about the present circumstances, showing the temporary nature of these things and the perpetual nature of those things, setting against the labors the prizes, against the tortures the crowns, against the pains the rewards, teaching what the present life is and what the future life is, and how great the distance between each is, and that it is altogether necessary to die; for even if we do not bring our life to an end in this manner, being altogether compelled by the law of nature, a little later at least we shall depart from these bodies. By urging these things and things like these, he raised up the weakened hands, he steadied the paralyzed knees, he brought back the fugitives, he cast out cowardice, he drove away anguish, he instilled courage, instead of cowards he made them eager, instead of gazelles and deer he made them lions breathing much strength, he welded together the army of Christ, he transferred the shame that was among us onto the heads of the enemies. The devil then, seeing that a sudden change had occurred, and that those who yesterday and the day before feared him and trembled now laughed at him and dared against him, stripping themselves for the dangers, leaping upon the torture chambers, and knowing the one responsible, leaving all aside, he breathed wholly against that one from then on, moving all his power and his madness against this blessed head. And what does he do? Observe the wickedness. He did not lead him to tortures, he did not cut off his head; for the time that had passed taught him that all these things happened in vain and to no purpose. For not only did he not cut short the eagerness of those who had believed, but he increased it more, and made it greater and hotter. I spread coals underneath, he says, but they ran as upon roses; I kindled fire, but they threw themselves as into springs of cold waters; I tore their sides, and cut deep furrows, and brought down streams of blood, but they adorned themselves as if flowing all around with gold; I hurled them down cliffs, and sank them into the sea, but they were disposed not as going down into the deep, but as going up into heaven itself, leaping and rejoicing, and as if dancing in a sacred procession, and playing in a green meadow, so each one snatched the punishments, not as punishments, but taking them as spring flowers, and being crowned, and by the excess of their own eagerness they anticipated my punishments. What then should be done, he says? Should I cut off this man's head? But what he prays for, this happens, and the disciples receive a greater exhortation through deeds; for he exhorted that the death of martyrs is not death, but life having no end, and especially for this one must endure all things, and that it is necessary to despise death. If then I cut off the head, and he bears nobly what has happened, through deeds he will teach them more clearly that thus it is necessary to despise death, and he will raise up their thoughts more, and having died he will breathe more eagerness into them.

choices.why: ὑποβρύχιος means 'under water, submerged'; the participle with γινομένων expresses an ongoing state of being overwhelmed, fitting the storm imagery.
αἴρω means 'to lift up, raise'; the storm is intensifying, not calming, matching the escalating danger.

choices.english: securing those who were standing with prayers
choices.why: ἀσφαλίζω means 'to make secure, to steady'; he is actively strengthening those already standing, not merely making them firm as a completed action.
rejected: making firm those who stood with prayers
he made those who were standing firm with prayers

choices.term: ἀντὶ δορκάδων καὶ ἐλάφων λέοντας ἀπειργάσατο
choices.english: instead of gazelles and deer he made them lions
choices.why: The contrast of timid animals with lions captures the transformation from fear to boldness; 'made them' preserves the active work of Romanus.
rejected: he turned gazelles and deer into lions
from gazelles and deer he produced lions

choices.english: he welded together the army of Christ
choices.why: συγκροτέω means 'to hammer together, to weld, to organize'; the military metaphor fits the context of spiritual warfare.
rejected: he assembled the camp of Christ
he united the army of Christ

choices.why: ἐπαποδύομαι means 'to strip oneself for action, to gird oneself'; it conveys eager preparation for combat, not mere approach.

pass_b_english: At that time, then, when many were being submerged, and the storm was rising, and many were suffering shipwreck, this blessed Romanus came into their midst. He did not immediately consider how to throw himself into the dangers, but first gathered together those who were afraid, those who had collapsed, those who had betrayed their own salvation. He encouraged them, he prepared them to fight back, raising up those who had fallen and securing those who were standing with prayers, exhortations, and counsels. He spoke at length about things to come and things present, showing the temporary nature of these and the permanence of those, setting rewards against labors, crowns against tortures, prizes against pains. He taught what the present life is and what the life to come is, how great the distance between the two, and that death is absolutely necessary. For even if we do not end our life in this way, we will certainly be compelled by the law of nature to depart from these bodies a little later.

By urging these things and others like them, he lifted up the weakened hands, he steadied the paralyzed knees, he brought back the fugitives, he cast out cowardice, he drove away anguish, he instilled courage. Instead of cowards he made them eager; instead of gazelles and deer he made them lions breathing with great strength. He welded together the army of Christ, and he turned the shame that was ours against the heads of the enemy.

So when the devil saw that a sudden transformation had taken place—that those who yesterday and the day before had feared him and trembled before him were now laughing at him and daring against him, stripping themselves for the dangers, leaping upon the torture chambers—and when he recognized the one responsible, he abandoned everyone else and breathed entirely against that man, moving all his power and madness against that blessed head.

And what does he do? Observe his wickedness. He did not bring him to tortures; he did not cut off his head. For the time that had passed had taught him that all these things were done in vain and to no purpose. Not only had they not cut short the eagerness of those who believed, but they had increased it further and made it greater and more fervent. “I spread coals underneath,” he says, “but they ran as if on roses. I kindled fire, but they threw themselves in as if into springs of cold water. I tore their sides and cut deep furrows and brought down streams of blood, but they adorned themselves as if they were being drenched on every side with gold. I hurled them from cliffs and plunged them into the sea, but they were not like people going down into the deep; they were like people going up into heaven itself, leaping and rejoicing, dancing as if in a sacred procession, playing as if in a green meadow. Each one seized the punishments in this way—not as punishments, but as spring flowers, being crowned, and by the excess of their own eagerness they outstripped my punishments.”

“What then should be done?” he says. “Should I cut off this man’s head? But what he prays for is what happens, and his disciples receive greater exhortation through deeds. For he has urged that the death of martyrs is not death, but life without end, and that above all one must endure everything for this, and that one must despise death. If then I cut off his head, and he bears what happens nobly, he will teach them more clearly through deeds that death must be despised in this way, and he will raise their spirits even more, and by dying he will breathe greater eagerness into them.”

problems.quote: he transferred the shame that was among us onto the heads of the enemy
problems.source_quote: τὴν αἰσχύνην τὴν παρ' ἡμῖν εἰς τὰς τῶν πολεμίων μετήνεγκε κεφαλάς
problems.why: μετηνεγκε means 'turned/redirected,' not 'transferred' as if moving an object; the shame became the enemy's.
problems.fix: he turned the shame that was ours against the heads of the enemy

edits.old: he transferred the shame that was among us onto the heads of the enemy
edits.new: he turned the shame that was ours against the heads of the enemy

fixed: Changed 'transferred' to 'turned' to reflect μετήνεγκε as redirecting the shame against the enemy rather than moving it as an object.

last_rejected.quote: those who had betrayed their own salvation
last_rejected.why: Source means those who were betraying (imperfective aspect), not those who had already done so.
last_rejected.ruling: Aorist participle προδόντας is perfective ('having betrayed'), not imperfective. English correctly renders completed action.

last_rejected.why: The devil's speech is not marked as such in English; readers may miss these are the devil's words.
last_rejected.fix: Add 'the devil says' or similar attribution before the quoted speech.
last_rejected.ruling: Quotation marks and 'he says' clearly mark the devil's speech; readers will not miss it.

last_rejected.why: ἐπαποδύομαι means 'stripping off armor to fight,' not 'stripping themselves for'—implies undressing, not girding for battle.
last_rejected.fix: stripping off their armor for the fight, or girding themselves for combat
last_rejected.ruling: ἐπαποδύομαι means 'strip oneself'; 'stripping themselves for dangers' is valid, not undressing error.

last_rejected.why: συνεκρότησε means 'he rallied/mustered/held together,' not 'welded'—suggests military assembly, not metalwork.
last_rejected.fix: he rallied together, or he held firm
last_rejected.ruling: συνεκρότησε = 'assembled/rallied'; 'welded together' is acceptable figurative rendering of unifying.

last_rejected.why: ἔπνευσεν here means 'he directed his blast/attack,' not 'breathed'—metaphor of storm/wind, not respiration.
last_rejected.fix: he directed his full blast against that man
last_rejected.ruling: ἔπνευσεν metaphorically means 'breathed/blew against'; 'breathed against' is valid range.

last_rejected.quote: he will breathe greater eagerness into them
last_rejected.source_quote: πλείονα αὐτοῖς ἐμπνεύσει τελευτήσας τὴν προθυμίαν
last_rejected.why: ἐμπνεύσει means 'he will inspire/infuse,' not 'breathe into'—metaphor of inspiration, not literal breathing.
last_rejected.fix: by dying he will inspire greater eagerness in them
last_rejected.ruling: ἐμπνεύσει = 'inspire/breathe into'; 'breathe eagerness into' is valid metaphor, not literal error.
